title: Work Life Balance
subtitle: Talk about French working culture, career change, and negotiating better conditions

lessons.title: Le rythme de travail
lessons.description: Describe French working culture — hours, holidays, and the rhythm of a working week — using comparatives and impersonal expressions.

blocks.heading: The 35-hour week and legal hours
blocks.body: French law sets the legal working week at 35 hours; anything beyond that is paid as overtime (heures supplémentaires) or converted into extra days off (RTT). Most full-time contracts still say 39 heures with RTT days added on top, so the real rhythm varies a lot between companies.

examples.french: En France, la durée légale du travail est de trente-cinq heures par semaine.
examples.english: In France, the legal working week is thirty-five hours.

examples.french: Elle travaille trente-neuf heures et récupère des jours de RTT.
examples.english: She works thirty-nine hours and earns RTT days off in return.

examples.french: Les heures supplémentaires sont mieux payées que les heures normales.
examples.english: Overtime hours are paid better than normal hours.

examples.french: Il est rare de travailler le week-end dans ce secteur.
examples.english: It's rare to work on weekends in this sector.

examples.french: Le rythme de travail dépend beaucoup de l'entreprise.
examples.english: The pace of work depends a lot on the company.

blocks.tip: "RTT" (réduction du temps de travail) are extra days off earned for working beyond 35 hours — ask a French colleague how many they get a year and you'll start a real conversation.

blocks.heading: Congés payés and jours fériés
blocks.body: Full-time employees in France get at least five weeks of paid leave (congés payés) a year, on top of about eleven public holidays (jours fériés). Many businesses slow down or close entirely in August, when a large share of the country takes its main summer break.

examples.french: Chaque salarié a droit à cinq semaines de congés payés par an.
examples.english: Every employee is entitled to five weeks of paid leave a year.

examples.french: Le 1er mai est un jour férié presque partout dans le monde.
examples.english: May 1st is a public holiday almost everywhere in the world.

examples.french: Beaucoup d'entreprises ferment la moitié du mois d'août.
examples.english: Many companies close for half of August.

examples.french: Elle pose ses congés trois mois à l'avance.
examples.english: She books her leave three months in advance.
examples.note: poser un congé = to request leave

examples.french: On dit souvent que les Français aiment prendre du temps pour souffler.
examples.english: People often say the French like to take time to catch their breath.

blocks.heading: Comparing rhythms and habits
blocks.body: To describe how work rhythms differ — between countries, jobs, or generations — French relies heavily on comparatives (plus/moins/aussi ... que) and superlatives (le plus, le moins). This lets you frame opinions clearly: what's more common, less stressful, or the most balanced.

examples.french: Le rythme de travail y est plus détendu qu'ailleurs.
examples.english: The pace of work there is more relaxed than elsewhere.

examples.french: Les cadres ont souvent moins de temps libre que les employés.
examples.english: Executives often have less free time than employees.

examples.french: C'est le secteur où l'équilibre est le plus difficile à trouver.
examples.english: It's the sector where balance is hardest to find.

examples.french: Le télétravail rend la journée aussi flexible que possible.
examples.english: Remote work makes the day as flexible as possible.

blocks.heading: Comparatives and superlatives
blocks.body: Use plus/moins/aussi + adjective + que to compare two things, and le/la/les plus (or moins) + adjective for the superlative. With verbs, use plus/moins/autant que after the verb instead. These structures are essential for describing which job, sector, or country has a better rhythm.

examples.french: Ce poste est plus exigeant que le précédent.
examples.english: This job is more demanding than the previous one.

examples.french: Le télétravail est aussi productif que le travail au bureau.
examples.english: Remote work is as productive as office work.

examples.french: Elle a moins de congés que ses collègues allemands.
examples.english: She has less leave than her German colleagues.

examples.french: C'est le secteur le plus flexible que je connaisse.
examples.english: It's the most flexible sector I know.

examples.french: Il travaille autant que moi, mais il se repose davantage.
examples.english: He works as much as I do, but he rests more.

blocks.tip: "Bon" and "bien" have irregular comparatives: meilleur(e) (better, adjective) and mieux (better, adverb) — never say "plus bon".

blocks.heading: Impersonal expressions + infinitive or subjunctive
blocks.body: Impersonal expressions like il est courant de, il est normal de, il est rare de are followed by the infinitive when there's no specific subject. When you want to express a personal necessity or judgement about someone in particular, French switches to il faut que / il est important que + subjunctive.

examples.french: Il est courant de prendre une pause déjeuner d'une heure.
examples.english: It's common to take a one-hour lunch break.

examples.french: Il est rare de travailler le samedi dans ce métier.
examples.english: It's rare to work on Saturdays in this profession.

examples.french: Il faut que les salariés posent leurs congés à l'avance.
examples.english: Employees need to book their leave in advance.

examples.french: Il est important que chacun trouve son propre équilibre.
examples.english: It's important that everyone finds their own balance.

examples.french: Il vaut mieux qu'on respecte les horaires de la réunion.
examples.english: It's better that we respect the meeting times.

blocks.tip: Trigger word: whenever a specific person becomes the subject of the second verb, switch from infinitive to "que + subjunctive".

passages.title: Le rythme de travail à la française
passages.french:
En France, la durée légale du travail est fixée à trente-cinq heures par semaine, mais la réalité varie beaucoup selon les entreprises.
Beaucoup de salariés travaillent en fait trente-neuf heures et récupèrent la différence sous forme de jours de RTT.
Chaque année, ils ont aussi droit à cinq semaines de congés payés, ce qui est plus généreux que dans de nombreux autres pays.
L'été, en particulier au mois d'août, un grand nombre d'entreprises tournent au ralenti, voire ferment complètement.
Le déjeuner occupe également une place importante : la pause de midi dure souvent une heure entière, loin du sandwich avalé devant l'ordinateur.
Depuis quelques années, le télétravail a changé le quotidien de millions de personnes.
Il permet d'éviter les transports, mais il floute aussi la frontière entre le bureau et la maison.
Certains salariés avouent qu'ils ont plus de mal à décompresser depuis qu'ils travaillent chez eux.
D'autres, au contraire, disent que leur charge de travail a enfin trouvé un équilibre acceptable.
Les syndicats, de leur côté, continuent de négocier pour que les horaires restent raisonnables.
Ils rappellent régulièrement qu'un bon rythme de travail profite autant à la santé qu'à la productivité.
Trouver l'équilibre reste, malgré tout, un défi quotidien pour beaucoup de Français.
passages.english:
In France, the legal working week is set at thirty-five hours, but the reality varies a lot from company to company.
Many employees actually work thirty-nine hours and get the difference back as RTT days off.
Each year, they are also entitled to five weeks of paid leave, which is more generous than in many other countries.
In summer, especially in August, a large number of companies slow right down, or even close completely.
Lunch also holds an important place: the midday break often lasts a full hour, far from a sandwich eaten in front of a computer.
In recent years, remote work has changed the daily life of millions of people.
It avoids commuting, but it also blurs the line between the office and home.
Some employees admit they find it harder to unwind since they started working from home.
Others, on the contrary, say their workload has finally found an acceptable balance.
Unions, for their part, keep negotiating so that hours stay reasonable.
They regularly point out that a good work rhythm benefits both health and productivity.
Finding the balance remains, nonetheless, a daily challenge for many French people.

lessons.title: La reconversion
lessons.description: Narrate a career-change story using relative pronouns and a mix of imparfait and passé composé.

blocks.heading: What is a reconversion?
blocks.body: A reconversion professionnelle is a deliberate career change — often a complete switch of field, not just a new employer. It usually starts with a bilan de compétences (a skills assessment) and involves weighing a stable job against a more meaningful but riskier path.

examples.french: Après quinze ans dans la finance, il a entamé une reconversion.
examples.english: After fifteen years in finance, he began a career change.

examples.french: Elle a fait un bilan de compétences avant de se reconvertir.
examples.english: She did a skills assessment before retraining.

examples.french: Se reconvertir demande souvent du courage et des économies.
examples.english: Retraining often requires courage and savings.

examples.french: Beaucoup de reconversions passent par une nouvelle formation.
examples.english: Many career changes go through new training.

examples.french: Il a quitté un poste stable pour suivre sa passion.
examples.english: He left a stable job to follow his passion.

blocks.tip: "Se reconvertir dans" + field (se reconvertir dans la pâtisserie) — "dans" is the preposition French uses here, not "en" or "à".

blocks.heading: The turning point: le déclic
blocks.body: French career-change stories almost always mention un déclic — a sudden realization or trigger moment. This is often described with venir de + infinitive (to have just done something) or with a short imparfait scene setting up the moment of change.

examples.french: J'ai eu un déclic le jour où j'ai perdu mon emploi.
examples.english: I had a moment of realization the day I lost my job.

examples.french: Elle venait de terminer un projet épuisant quand elle a tout remis en question.
examples.english: She had just finished an exhausting project when she questioned everything.

examples.french: Ce fut un vrai tournant dans sa carrière.
examples.english: It was a real turning point in his career.

examples.french: Il ne savait pas encore ce qu'il voulait, mais il savait ce qu'il ne voulait plus.
examples.english: He didn't know yet what he wanted, but he knew what he no longer wanted.

blocks.heading: Talking about risk, failure, and success
blocks.body: Reconversion stories balance doubt and determination: oser (to dare), prendre un risque (to take a risk), échouer/l'échec (to fail/failure), and réussir (to succeed) all recur. Persévérer captures the long middle stretch between the decision and the result.

examples.english: She dared to start everything over at forty.

examples.french: Aujourd'hui, elle dit s'être enfin épanouie dans son travail.

blocks.heading: Relative pronouns: qui, que, dont, où
blocks.body: Qui replaces a subject, que replaces a direct object, dont replaces a phrase with de (parler de, avoir besoin de, être fier de), and où replaces a place or a time. These pronouns let you link two short sentences into one richer one — exactly what career-change stories need.

examples.french: C'est un métier qui me passionne vraiment.
examples.english: It's a job that I'm truly passionate about.

examples.french: La formation que j'ai suivie a duré six mois.
examples.english: The training I took lasted six months.

examples.french: C'est le domaine dont je rêvais depuis toujours.
examples.english: It's the field I had always dreamed of.

examples.french: Je me souviens du jour où j'ai démissionné.
examples.english: I remember the day when I resigned.

examples.french: L'entreprise où je travaille maintenant est bien plus petite.
examples.english: The company where I now work is much smaller.

blocks.tip: Quick test: if the missing word would need "de" before it in the simple sentence (j'ai besoin DE ce déclic), use dont.

blocks.heading: Narrating a turning point
blocks.body: A good reconversion story sets the scene with imparfait (how things were, ongoing feelings) and marks the decisive event with passé composé. Décider de + infinitive and venir de + infinitive are the two workhorse structures for the moment things changed.

examples.french: Je travaillais dans la finance depuis dix ans quand j'ai eu mon déclic.
examples.english: I had been working in finance for ten years when I had my realization.

examples.french: J'étais fatiguée, je ne dormais plus bien — alors j'ai décidé d'arrêter.
examples.english: I was tired, I wasn't sleeping well anymore — so I decided to stop.

examples.french: Il venait de perdre son emploi quand l'idée lui est venue.
examples.english: He had just lost his job when the idea came to him.

examples.french: Elle a décidé de tout recommencer, même si elle avait peur.
examples.english: She decided to start everything over, even though she was scared.

blocks.tip: Imparfait paints the background; passé composé cuts in with the single decisive action — that contrast is what makes the story land.

passages.title: Le déclic de Sophie
passages.french:
Sophie avait trente-quatre ans quand elle a quitté son poste d'avocate dans un grand cabinet parisien.
Pendant dix ans, elle travaillait souvent le week-end et rentrait tard tous les soirs.
Elle gagnait bien sa vie, mais elle se sentait de plus en plus vide.
Un dimanche, alors qu'elle préparait un gâteau pour des amis, elle a eu un déclic.
Elle s'est rendu compte que ces heures passées en cuisine étaient les seules où elle se sentait vraiment elle-même.
Elle a alors fait un bilan de compétences, puis elle a osé poser sa démission.
Beaucoup de gens autour d'elle ont douté de sa décision.
Elle a suivi une formation de pâtissière pendant huit mois, qu'elle a financée avec ses économies.
La première année a été difficile : elle travaillait plus qu'avant, pour un salaire bien plus petit.
Mais elle dit aujourd'hui qu'elle ne regrette rien.
« Je gagne moins, mais je me suis enfin épanouie dans un métier qui a du sens pour moi », explique-t-elle.
Sa reconversion est devenue, pour ses anciens collègues, un vrai sujet de conversation.
passages.english:
Sophie was thirty-four when she left her job as a lawyer at a large Parisian firm.
For ten years, she often worked weekends and came home late every evening.
She earned a good living, but she felt increasingly empty.
One Sunday, while making a cake for friends, she had a moment of realization.
She realized that those hours spent in the kitchen were the only ones where she truly felt like herself.
She then did a skills assessment, and dared to hand in her resignation.
Many people around her doubted her decision.
She took an eight-month pastry-making course, which she funded with her savings.
The first year was difficult: she worked more than before, for a much smaller salary.
But today she says she has no regrets.
"I earn less, but I've finally flourished in a job that has meaning for me," she explains.
Her career change became, for her former colleagues, a real topic of conversation.

lessons.title: Négocier au travail
lessons.description: Ask politely for flexible hours or remote work using the conditional and the subjunctive after expressions of wish and necessity.

blocks.heading: Opening the conversation politely
blocks.body: French workplace negotiation almost always starts softer than in English: you signal the topic before making the actual request, and you use the conditional to sound tentative rather than demanding. "Est-ce que je pourrais vous parler de..." is a very common opener before asking for anything.

examples.french: Est-ce que je pourrais vous parler de mes horaires ?
examples.english: Could I talk to you about my hours?

examples.french: J'aimerais aborder un sujet avec vous, si vous avez un moment.
examples.english: I'd like to bring up a topic with you, if you have a moment.

examples.french: Auriez-vous cinq minutes pour discuter d'une demande ?
examples.english: Would you have five minutes to discuss a request?

examples.french: Je voudrais vous soumettre une idée concernant le télétravail.
examples.english: I would like to put an idea to you concerning remote work.

examples.french: Ce serait le bon moment pour en parler ?
examples.english: Would this be a good time to talk about it?

blocks.tip: In French offices, "vous" is the default with a manager unless they explicitly invite "tu" — keep it formal until told otherwise.

blocks.heading: Making the request with the conditional
blocks.body: The conditionnel présent softens requests: je voudrais, pourriez-vous, serait-il possible de. It signals politeness without sounding weak — French negotiation values a confident but courteous tone rather than blunt demands.

examples.french: Je voudrais travailler à distance deux jours par semaine.
examples.english: I would like to work remotely two days a week.

examples.french: Pourriez-vous envisager des horaires plus flexibles pour moi ?
examples.english: Could you consider more flexible hours for me?

examples.french: Serait-il possible de décaler mon arrivée à neuf heures trente ?
examples.english: Would it be possible to shift my start time to nine thirty?

examples.french: J'aimerais qu'on trouve un compromis qui convienne à tout le monde.
examples.english: I would like us to find a compromise that suits everyone.

examples.french: Ce serait plus simple pour moi si je pouvais partir un peu plus tôt le vendredi.
examples.english: It would be simpler for me if I could leave a bit earlier on Fridays.

blocks.heading: Subjunctive after wish and necessity
blocks.body: Verbs and expressions of wish, wanting, or necessity — vouloir que, aimerais que, il faudrait que — trigger the subjunctive in the clause that follows, as long as the subject changes. This lets you frame a negotiation as a shared need rather than a one-sided order.

examples.french: Je voudrais que nous trouvions un accord avant vendredi.
examples.english: I would like us to reach an agreement before Friday.

examples.french: Il faudrait que vous acceptiez au moins un jour de télétravail.
examples.english: You would need to accept at least one day of remote work.

examples.french: J'aimerais que ma charge de travail soit réévaluée.
examples.english: I would like my workload to be reassessed.

examples.french: Il faut que la direction comprenne notre point de vue.
examples.english: Management needs to understand our point of view.

blocks.tip: No subject change, no subjunctive: "je voudrais partir tôt" (infinitive) but "je voudrais qu'il parte tôt" (subjunctive, different subject).

blocks.heading: Building the conditionnel présent
blocks.body: The conditionnel présent is formed from the futur stem (usually the infinitive, minus a final -e for -re verbs) plus the imparfait endings: -ais, -ais, -ait, -ions, -iez, -aient. Pouvoir, vouloir, and être have irregular stems that are worth memorizing for negotiation language.

examples.english: I would like, we would like, they would like...

examples.french: Seriez-vous d'accord pour en discuter demain ?
examples.english: Would you be willing to discuss it tomorrow?

blocks.tip: "Pourriez-vous" is the single most useful phrase for polite workplace requests — learn it as one block.

blocks.heading: The subjunctive present of key verbs
blocks.body: Most verbs form the subjunctive from the ils-form of the present (ils parlent → que je parle), but être, avoir, faire, pouvoir, and vouloir are irregular and appear constantly in negotiation language.

examples.french: que je sois, que tu sois, qu'il soit...
examples.english: that I be, that you be, that he be...

examples.french: que j'aie, qu'elle ait, que nous ayons...
examples.english: that I have, that she have, that we have...

examples.french: il faut que je fasse cette demande moi-même.
examples.english: I need to make this request myself.

examples.french: je voudrais que vous puissiez accepter ce compromis.
examples.english: I would like you to be able to accept this compromise.

examples.french: il faudrait que la direction veuille bien nous écouter.
examples.english: Management would need to be willing to listen to us.

blocks.tip: These five irregular subjunctives (être, avoir, faire, pouvoir, vouloir) are worth drilling on their own — everything else follows the regular pattern.

passages.title: Une négociation réussie
passages.french:
Karim travaille dans la même entreprise depuis quatre ans et il aimerait plus de flexibilité.
Un lundi matin, il demande un rendez-vous à sa responsable, Mme Lefèvre.
« Bonjour, est-ce que je pourrais vous parler de mes horaires ? » commence-t-il.
« Bien sûr, asseyez-vous, je vous écoute », répond-elle.
« Je voudrais travailler à distance deux jours par semaine, si c'est possible. »
« Pourquoi cette demande maintenant ? » demande Mme Lefèvre, un peu surprise.
« Le trajet me prend deux heures par jour, et je pense que je serais plus efficace chez moi. »
Karim explique aussi que sa charge de travail est plus facile à gérer sans les interruptions du bureau.
Mme Lefèvre hésite, puis propose un compromis : un jour de télétravail, à l'essai pendant deux mois.
« Si les résultats sont bons, on pourra en reparler », précise-t-elle.
Karim accepte avec plaisir ; ce n'est pas exactement ce qu'il voulait, mais c'est un bon début.
Deux mois plus tard, grâce à ses bons résultats, il obtient finalement ses deux jours de télétravail.
passages.english:
Karim has worked at the same company for four years and would like more flexibility.
One Monday morning, he asks his manager, Mrs Lefèvre, for a meeting.
"Hello, could I talk to you about my hours?" he begins.
"Of course, sit down, I'm listening," she replies.
"I would like to work remotely two days a week, if that's possible."
"Why this request now?" asks Mrs Lefèvre, a little surprised.
"The commute takes me two hours a day, and I think I would be more efficient at home."
Karim also explains that his workload is easier to manage without office interruptions.
Mrs Lefèvre hesitates, then proposes a compromise: one day of remote work, on trial for two months.
"If the results are good, we can talk about it again," she specifies.
Karim accepts happily; it's not exactly what he wanted, but it's a good start.
Two months later, thanks to his good results, he finally gets his two days of remote work.
